**GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD - General Certificate of Education Examination. JUNE 2025, ADVANCED LEVEL. English Language, Paper 2 (0730).**

Answer your questions either exclusively from **PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS)** or from **PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS)**.

**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - Duration: Two and a Quarter Hours.** Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION (Section A: Composition, Section B: Prescribed Texts, Section C: Creative Writing). ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you no marks.

**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - Duration: Three Hours.** Instructions to candidates: Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you little or no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you little or no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - SECTION B: PRESCRIBED TEXTS (20 MARKS)**

Answer ONE question only.

**1.** Read the following poem and answer the questions below it.

''IF WE MUST DIE''

If we must die, let it not be like hogs
Hunted and penned in an ***inglorious spot***,
While round us bark the mad and hungry dogs,
Making their mock at our ***accursed lot***.  [5]

If we must die, O let us ***nobly die***,
So that our precious blood may not be shed
In vain; then even the monsters will we defy
Shall be constrained to honor us through dead!
O kinsmen! We must meet the common foe!  [10]
Though far outnumbered let us show us brave,
And for their thousand blows deal one death - blow
What though before us lies the open grave?
Like men we'll face the murderous, **cowardly pack**
Pressed to the wall, dying, but fighting back.  [15]

Les repères imprimés (5), (10), (15) sont placés en regard des vers 4, 9 et 14 ; les références du sujet (L.2, L.5, L.6, L.15) comptent en réalité la ligne blanche entre les strophes et ne tombent pas exactement sur ces repères (« accursed lot » est au vers 4) : les expressions sont identifiées par leurs mots.

III (phrasal verbs de la première strophe) : la strophe ne contient qu'un phrasal verb sûr (penned in) ; la seconde réponse attendue par le jury n'est pas connue, le corrigé le dit et propose « fighting back » en dehors de la strophe. questions.enonce_markdown: **I.** In a paragraph, say what you consider to be the poet's message. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model paragraph (77 words)**

The poet's message is that people who are oppressed and hunted must not accept death passively, like animals driven into a trap. If death cannot be avoided, they should face it bravely, united as kinsmen, and die fighting so that their blood is not shed in vain. Such a heroic resistance wins the respect even of their enemies, who will be forced to honour them. Dignity in the face of death matters more than survival through humiliation.

**Marking**: 2 marks for the central idea (die bravely and with honour, fighting back, not like hogs), 2 marks for support and expression (unity of the kinsmen, blood not shed in vain, enemies forced to honour them, a single well-written paragraph).

questions.enonce_markdown:
**II.** Give the meaning in context of the following words/expressions: (4 marks)

(i) ... *inglorious spot* ... (L.2)

(ii) ... *accursed lot* ... (L.5)

(iii) ... *nobly die*, ... (L.6)

(iv) ... *cowardly pack* ... (L.15)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Meanings in context (1 mark each)**

| Expression | Meaning in context |
|---|---|
| (i) *inglorious spot* | A shameful, dishonourable place or situation, without any glory, where the oppressed are cornered and killed like animals. |
| (ii) *accursed lot* | The wretched, cursed fate or condition of the oppressed, which their enemies mock. |
| (iii) *nobly die* | To die bravely and with dignity, in a worthy cause (resisting the enemy), instead of cowering. |
| (iv) *cowardly pack* | The enemy group, who attack together like a pack of dogs and murder others because they lack courage when alone. |

**Method**: give the meaning the words have in this poem (who is speaking, about whom), not only a dictionary definition.
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: **III.** Pick out two phrasal verbs from the first stanza. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Answer**: *penned in* (line 2: 'Hunted and **penned in** an inglorious spot'; to pen in = to shut or trap in a small place).

A phrasal verb is a verb followed by an adverb or a preposition whose meaning is different from that of the verb alone. The first stanza contains only one clear example, *penned in*. The other expression a candidate may offer from the stanza, *bark ... round us*, is not a recognised phrasal verb, so it should not be given. A second phrasal verb is found at the end of the poem: *fighting back* (to fight back = to resist an attack).

**Mark scheme**: 1 mark for each correct phrasal verb. A candidate who gives *penned in* and justifies a second choice correctly is rewarded.

questions.enonce_markdown: **IV.** Pick out four adverbs and change them to nouns. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Answer** (each adverb from the poem with the noun formed from it; 1 mark each)

| Adverb in the poem | Noun |
|---|---|
| *nobly* (L.6) | nobility |
| *far* (as in 'far outnumbered') | distance (or farness) |
| *not* (as in 'let it not be like hogs') | negation |
| *in vain* (adverbial phrase) | vanity (or futility) |

**Method**: first decide the word's job in the sentence (an adverb tells how, when, where or to what degree), then use the suffix that forms the noun (-ly adverb to adjective to noun: nobly, noble, nobility). Other adverbs of the poem that may be accepted: *even*, *then*, *back*.
themes: A Level English - parts of speech

questions.enonce_markdown: **V.** Show how the theme of bravery in the poem is reflected in any other **two** prescribed texts. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Method answer: the prescribed texts are not available here, so no detail of any work is given. Apply this method to two other texts you have studied.**

**What 'bravery' means in the poem**: facing a stronger enemy openly, refusing humiliation, acting together as kinsmen, and accepting the risk of death for honour.

**Plan (about 3 marks per text)**

1. One sentence on the poem's idea of bravery, then name the first text with its writer.
2. First text: who shows bravery (a character, a speaker or a community), what they do, what it costs them, and the result. Give one precise event or a short quotation.
3. Second text: the same steps. Choose a text where bravery takes a different form (for example moral courage, endurance or leadership) so that the two paragraphs are not repetitive.
4. A closing sentence on what the three texts (the poem and the two others) say together about courage.

**Marking grid (indicative; the paper prints 6 marks)**

| Criterion | What earns the marks |
|---|---|
| Relevance | Each text is clearly linked with the theme of bravery |
| Evidence | A precise event, character or quotation from EXACTLY two other texts |
| Expression | Clear paragraphs, formal register, correct grammar |

**Common mistakes**

1. Retelling the story instead of showing the theme.
2. Using the poem again, or using only one other text.
3. Naming a text but giving no precise evidence.
